subject: psychology
title: Social Influence: Studies and Applications
welcome_lead: Step into Asch's lab, Milgram's shock generator and Kitty Genovese's street.
meta_desc: GCSE Psychology adventure on classic social influence studies: Asch, Milgram and bystander effect.
final_note: You can cite three landmark studies on social influence.

concepts.def: 1963 obedience test using fake electric shocks.
People help less when others are present.
Sharing blame so no individual acts.

walkthroughs.body_html: One real participant judged line length with 7 confederates who gave wrong answers. The mean conformity rate was 37%, and around 75% conformed at least once. Mostly NSI — going along to fit in.

Participants gave (fake) electric shocks up to 450V on the orders of an experimenter in a lab coat. 65% went to the maximum 450V. The study showed ordinary people obey destructive orders under authority.

Following the 1964 Kitty Genovese case, Latané & Darley showed that more bystanders meant less help. They proposed diffusion of responsibility and pluralistic ignorance as causes of the bystander effect.
